passage: At the playschool's birthday circle, Miss set one big bowl of laddoos in the middle. "Share nicely." Suraj, five, saw Wasim grab two, so he grabbed three, fast, before they could go. Wasim grabbed four more. In a minute the bowl was empty. Little Pema, who was shy, got none and began to cry. Suraj looked at his sticky hands full of laddoos. He hadn't even wanted three. Miss knelt down. "What happened to the bowl?" Suraj mumbled, "Everybody took fast so nobody else could." Slowly, he put one laddoo in Pema's hand.

qa.q: How many laddoos did Suraj grab?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Suraj grab three laddoos so fast?
qa.a: He saw Wasim grab two and worried the laddoos would be gone if he waited.

qa.q: What could Miss try next time with a shared bowl?
qa.a: She could pass the bowl around so each child takes one per turn, so nobody feels they must grab first.

qa.q: What was it like for Pema when the bowl emptied?
qa.a: Pema, who was shy, got none and cried, left out because everyone rushed.

grounding: Young children at a shared bowl each grab quickly for fear the others will take it all, and the shared treat is gone before everyone gets some.

passage: I'm Jahnavi, and at my little brother Rafiq's fifth birthday I was in charge of the chocolate tin. I opened it in the middle of the rug and said, "Take some." For a second nobody moved. Then his friend Ivan grabbed a fistful, and every hand dived in at once. Rafiq pushed in too, stuffing chocolates into his pockets, his eyes on the others. The tin was empty in less than a minute. Two smaller kids got nothing. Rafiq had eleven chocolates and a smeared face, and he didn't look happy. He looked worried, as if someone might take them.

qa.q: How many chocolates did Rafiq end up with?
qa.a: Eleven chocolates.

qa.q: What does Rafiq's worried look suggest?
qa.a: He seemed afraid someone might take his chocolates, even though he had grabbed so many.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try the next time Jahnavi is in charge of the tin?
qa.a: Jahnavi could hand out chocolates one round at a time, so no one has to rush to get a share.

qa.q: How might the two smaller kids feel when the tin is empty?
qa.a: They probably feel left out and sad, having got nothing because they were slower.

grounding: An older sibling watches young children grab from a shared tin once one starts, emptying it so the slower ones get nothing.

passage: Monday. Nani set down a plate of mango slices for Nikita and her cousin Tanuja. Nikita grabbed five at once, before Tanuja could. Tanuja grabbed the rest. Nani came back to an empty plate and two sticky, cross girls. Wednesday. Same plate. Nikita's hand shot out, then stopped. But Tanuja was already reaching, so both grabbed, and a slice fell on the floor. Friday. Nani put the plate down and said, "One each, then wait." Nikita took one. Tanuja took one. Back and forth they went, counting. One slice was left. They looked at each other. "Halves?" said Tanuja.

qa.q: How many mango slices did Nikita grab on Monday?
qa.a: Five at once.

qa.q: Why did Nikita's hand stop and then grab anyway on Wednesday?
qa.a: She seemed to remember Monday, but when she saw Tanuja reaching she worried she'd miss out and grabbed anyway.

qa.q: What choice did Nani make on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Nani set a rule of one each, then wait, so neither girl had to rush to get her share.

qa.q: What might Tanuja be feeling when she offers 'Halves?'
qa.a: Tanuja seems relaxed and fair now, trusting that sharing the last slice will not leave her short.

grounding: Two young cousins grab from a shared plate because each fears the other will take it, until a simple turn-taking rule lets them share.

passage: "Last tray! Counter closes in five minutes!" the caterer shouted across the noisy wedding hall. Pradeep, five, ran to the kids' table, where a big steel tray of gulab jamun sat steaming. His cousin Chaitanya was already there, scooping with both hands. Pradeep piled four into his paper plate, then two more, fast, before they were gone. More children pushed in. In a minute the tray held only syrup. Little Guddi, three, arrived late and stared at it. Pradeep looked at his plate. Syrup was dripping through the paper onto his new shoes, and he couldn't eat even three.

qa.q: How many gulab jamun did Pradeep put in his plate altogether?
qa.a: Pradeep piled four into his paper plate, then two more, so six gulab jamun.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep grab so many so quickly?
qa.a: He was afraid the tray would be empty soon, because the caterer said it was the last tray and Chaitanya was already scooping with both hands.

qa.q: What could the grown-ups have done when the last tray came out?
qa.a: They could have handed out two each to the children in a line, so nobody had to rush and grab before it was gone.

qa.q: How might Guddi feel when she reaches the table and finds only syrup?
qa.a: Guddi might feel left out and sad, because the older children took everything before she even got there.

grounding: A five-year-old at a wedding grabs far more sweets than he can eat because others are grabbing, and the shared tray is emptied before a small child gets any.

passage: On Diwali evening Aparna Aunty from 3B put a steel bowl of coconut barfi on the stair landing. "For all the building children!" she called, and went back inside. Rukmini, four, heard feet thundering down the stairs. She ran too. Big hands were in the bowl. Rukmini grabbed five pieces and pushed them into her frock pocket. The bowl was empty before old Mr Joshi from the ground floor even reached the landing. Later, Rukmini put her hand in her pocket. The barfi had turned into warm, crumbly mush. She licked her fingers and looked at the empty bowl.

qa.q: Where did Aparna Aunty put the bowl of barfi?
qa.a: She put it on the stair landing on Diwali evening, for all the building children.

qa.q: What was going through Rukmini's mind when she heard feet thundering down the stairs?
qa.a: She was worried the barfi would all go to the bigger children, so she hurried and took five pieces before anyone else could take them.

qa.q: What small step could have kept the barfi for everyone?
qa.a: If each child had taken one piece and waited, there would have been enough for everyone, including Mr Joshi, and nothing would have turned to mush.

qa.q: How might Aparna Aunty feel if she came out and saw the empty bowl?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a bit disappointed that her treat for all the children was gone in a rush, with some people getting none.

grounding: A four-year-old stuffs her pocket with shared sweets because others are grabbing, and the bowl empties before everyone gets a share.

passage:
Friday: At Santosh's fifth birthday, Mummy puts one big bowl of toffees on the mat. Santosh grabs two fistfuls. Reena, five, sees him and grabs fast too. In a minute the bowl is empty. Two little ones get nothing.
Sunday: Nani puts out a plate of chikki. Santosh and Reena both lunge. A piece falls and breaks.
Tuesday: At the park, Reena holds out her biscuit packet. Santosh reaches for three. Reena snatches it back. "You always take all!"

qa.q: How many children got nothing at the birthday?
qa.a: Two little ones got nothing.

qa.q: Why did Reena grab fast at the birthday?
qa.a: Reena was worried that if she waited, Santosh would take everything and she would get none.

qa.q: What could Mummy try next time with the toffees?
qa.a: Mummy could give each child a small plate or let them take turns, so no one feels they must grab to get any.

qa.q: How might the two little ones feel when the bowl was empty?
qa.a: They probably felt left out and sad, watching the older children take everything first.

grounding: Over a few days, young children grab quickly from shared bowls because waiting means others will take it, leaving the group's treats drained.

passage: The power went out at the wedding just as the aunties set down one bowl of laddoos for the children. In the dark, Damini, five, heard hands rustling. She grabbed four laddoos and stuffed two in her frock pocket. Abhinav, six, grabbed five. "If I don't, the big kids will take them," he whispered. When the lights came back, the bowl was bare. A little girl in a pink lehenga was crying; she'd got none. Damini looked at the squashed, sticky laddoos in her pocket, then at the crying girl.

qa.q: How many laddoos did Damini grab?
qa.a: Damini grabbed four laddoos.

qa.q: What was Abhinav worried about when he grabbed five?
qa.a: Abhinav was anxious that the big kids would take all the laddoos if he waited.

qa.q: What might help children share a bowl like this more fairly?
qa.a: An adult could hand out laddoos one by one, or count them out, so the children don't feel they must rush to get any.

qa.q: How might the girl in the pink lehenga see what happened?
qa.a: She likely felt sad and left out, seeing that others had grabbed so much that none was left for her.

grounding: In a dark, crowded wedding, children grab from a shared bowl because others might take it first, and the treats quickly run out.

passage: At the Saturday movie night on their Pune building's terrace, Mehak's mother set one big tub of popcorn between the six children. Uday, five, took a huge handful. Mehak, six, saw him and grabbed an even bigger one, spilling half on the mat. The others copied. In minutes the tub was empty, and the movie had just started. "I want more," Uday said. Mehak's mother shook her head. "That was all of it." Mehak held her one leftover kernel and frowned. Most of it was on the mat.

qa.q: How many children shared the tub of popcorn?
qa.a: The tub was set between the six children.

qa.q: What does Mehak's frown at her one leftover kernel suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt disappointed and a bit puzzled, realising that grabbing fast had left almost nothing to eat.

qa.q: How could Mehak's mother share the popcorn next time?
qa.a: She could give each child a small bowl, so no one has to grab and less is wasted on the floor.

qa.q: What was it like for Uday when he saw the empty tub?
qa.a: Uday felt let down and still hungry, wanting more when there was none left.

grounding: Children grab from a shared popcorn tub because others will take it, and the group's treat is used up and wasted.

passage:
"Lohri fire's ready!" Mamaji called from the courtyard.
Vaibhav ran out. On the charpai sat one steel bowl heaped with rewri and peanuts.
"That's for everyone," said Mama. "Bhupen, Vaibhav, the cousins, all of you."
Bhupen reached in first. Vaibhav watched his cousin's hand and grabbed with both of his, stuffing his kurta pockets.
"Vaibhav! Why so many?"
"Because Bhupen will finish it!"
"I was going to!" said Bhupen, grabbing more.
By the time the little cousins came, the bowl was empty. The smallest one started to cry.

qa.q: What was heaped in the steel bowl on the charpai?
qa.a: Rewri and peanuts were heaped in the steel bowl.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav grab with both hands and fill his pockets?
qa.a: He was worried that Bhupen would finish the bowl first, so he felt he had to grab before it was gone.

qa.q: How could Mama help the children share next time?
qa.a: Mama could give each child a small handful in turn, so nobody feels they must grab to get any.

qa.q: What is it like for the smallest cousin when the children reach the bowl?
qa.a: The smallest cousin finds the bowl empty and cries, missing out because the bigger children grabbed first.

grounding: Shows young children at a shared bowl of sweets grabbing fast because each fears the others will take it, leaving nothing for the rest.

passage:
Monsoon week, Sunflower group. Written by Rekha, class teacher.
The rain kept us indoors all morning, so I put one tin of cream biscuits on the mat for snack time. I said it was for the whole group.
Raghav looked at the tin, then at the others, and took five biscuits at once. He held them against his chest. Two more children did the same. Within a minute the tin was empty and three children had none.
Raghav told me, "If I wait, they eat it all."
Next I counted biscuits into a paper cup for each child, and we talked about the empty tin. Raghav gave one back.

qa.q: How many biscuits did Raghav take at once?
qa.a: Raghav took five biscuits at once.

qa.q: What was Raghav worried about when he held the biscuits against his chest?
qa.a: He was anxious that if he waited, the others would eat all of them and he would get none.

qa.q: What did the teacher's paper cups change?
qa.a: Each child knew a fair share was saved for them, so there was no reason to rush and grab.

qa.q: How might the three children with no biscuits feel?
qa.a: They would likely feel sad and left out, since the others' quick grabbing emptied the tin before they had a turn.

grounding: Illustrates a young child grabbing from a shared tin of treats out of fear the group will finish it, so several children are left with nothing.

passage:
On Makar Sankranti morning the village smelled of jaggery and sesame. Parveen's Ammi set a big plate of til laddoos on the courtyard step and said, "For all the children in the lane."
Damini came running from next door. She saw Parveen take two and hold them in her frock.
Damini grabbed four quickly. Parveen grabbed more. Then the boys from the other houses came and grabbed too.
The plate was empty before the kites were even out. Damini sat on the step with sticky fingers, and her tummy hurt. Two little girls from the end of the lane stood there with nothing.

qa.q: What did Parveen's Ammi set on the courtyard step?
qa.a: She set a big plate of til laddoos on the courtyard step.

qa.q: Why did Damini grab four laddoos so quickly?
qa.a: She saw Parveen taking some and felt worried there would be none left for her if she waited.

qa.q: What small step could Parveen's Ammi try next Sankranti?
qa.a: She could hand out laddoos one by one to each child, so nobody feels they must race.

qa.q: What is it like for the two little girls from the end of the lane?
qa.a: They arrive to an empty plate and feel left out, even though the laddoos were meant for all the children.

grounding: Shows children at a festival each grabbing from a shared plate of sweets for fear of missing out, so the shared plate is emptied and some get nothing.

passage: On the first morning of the Bayram holiday in Istanbul, Grandma set a big bowl of lokum on the low table and went to answer the door. Elif looked at Tariq. Tariq looked at Elif. Then both grabbed at once, fists full, then again, cheeks bulging. 'Save some!' Elif mumbled. 'You save some!' In a minute the bowl held only powdered sugar. When the cousins came in, there was nothing left. Elif felt sticky and strange. 'He took more,' she whispered. 'She did,' said Tariq.

qa.q: What did Grandma set on the low table?
qa.a: A big bowl of lokum.

qa.q: Why did Elif grab so quickly?
qa.a: Elif was worried Tariq would take it all if she waited, so she grabbed fast.

qa.q: How could Grandma set out sweets next time so everyone gets some?
qa.a: She could give each child a small plate with a fair share, or stay and let them take turns, so nobody feels they must rush.

qa.q: How might the cousins feel finding the bowl empty?
qa.a: The cousins would feel disappointed and left out, arriving to only powdered sugar.

grounding: During a holiday abroad two young children grab from a shared bowl until nothing is left for the others.

passage: At the playschool Christmas party, Miss Dsouza put one plate of star cookies in the middle of the circle. 'These are for everyone,' she said, and turned to fix the music. Ritu took two. Charu saw and took three. Ritu took three more. Soon every hand was grabbing, and the plate was bare before the song even started. Little Kunal, who had been waiting politely, began to cry. Charu looked at the crumbs in her lap. 'I took them because Ritu was taking them,' she said. Miss Dsouza sat down. 'Let's see how we can share the next plate.'

qa.q: What did Miss Dsouza put in the middle of the circle?
qa.a: One plate of star cookies.

qa.q: Why did Charu take three cookies?
qa.a: Charu worried there would be none left because Ritu was taking them, so she grabbed more.

qa.q: How could Miss Dsouza share the next plate fairly?
qa.a: She could count the cookies and let each child take one at a time round the circle, so nobody feels they must rush.

qa.q: How does Kunal feel when the plate is empty?
qa.a: Kunal, who waited politely, feels sad and left out, and begins to cry.

grounding: At a playschool party young children each grab quickly from a shared plate, emptying it for the group.

passage:
Diwali night: Nani gave Jagdish and his sister Yamini one big box of laddoos to share for the week. 'Take slowly,' she said.
Next morning: Yamini ate three before breakfast. Jagdish saw, and ate four, fast, before she could.
Two days later: the box was empty. Both wanted one after school, and there were none. Yamini cried; Jagdish sulked. 'You ate them!' 'You ate them too!' Nani sat down between them. 'Next time, shall we put two in each of your tins every day?' Both nodded, still sniffing.

qa.q: How many laddoos did Yamini eat before breakfast?
qa.a: Three before breakfast.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish eat four so fast?
qa.a: Jagdish worried Yamini would finish them first, so he hurried to get his share.

qa.q: Why is Nani's idea of two a day in each tin a good one?
qa.a: It shares the box fairly over the week, so nobody has to rush to get enough.

qa.q: How does Yamini feel after school when the box is empty?
qa.a: Yamini feels upset and disappointed, crying because there are no laddoos left.

grounding: Over a festival week two young siblings race to eat a shared box of sweets until none are left.

passage: Diwali evening, and the lights in Chachi's flat have just gone out. In the candle glow sits one steel bowl of kaju barfi for all six cousins. "Wait till I bring the plates," Chachi calls from the kitchen. Vishal, five, sees Sahil's hand slide toward the bowl. Quick as a squirrel, Vishal grabs four pieces and stuffs his pockets. Sahil grabs five. The littlest cousins grab too. When Chachi comes back with plates and a torch, the bowl is empty, and little Mishti is crying because she got none.

qa.q: What was in the steel bowl?
qa.a: Kaju barfi.

qa.q: Why did Vishal grab four pieces so fast?
qa.a: He was worried that if he waited, Sahil and the others would take it all, so he grabbed in a hurry.

qa.q: How could Chachi share the sweets next time?
qa.a: She could hand out the pieces herself, one each per round, so no child feels they must grab before it is gone.

qa.q: What is it like for little Mishti when the bowl comes back empty?
qa.a: Mishti feels sad and left out, crying because the quick grabbing left nothing for her.

grounding: Children with one shared bowl of sweets each grab fast for fear the others will take it, and the bowl is emptied.
